result: The authors used lineage tracing models (Tnfsf11aCre and Flt3Cre) to demonstrate that approximately 80% of cardiac macrophages are derived from yolk sac EMPs and 20% from definitive HSCs, concluding that the majority of resident cardiac macrophages are of early embryonic origin.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the use of 'state-of-the-art fate-mapping models' and recognize the lineage tracing data as solid evidence. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'solid with the use of the FIRE mouse model in combination with fate-mapping,' and Reviewer 2 highlights the 'major strength' of the fate-mapping approach. No concerns are raised about these foundational lineage tracing claims.

result: The authors validated the ΔFIRE mouse model by confirming ~90% reduction in cardiac macrophages (specifically EMP-derived) while monocytes and neutrophils remain unaltered, establishing this as a model to selectively study resident macrophages.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the ΔFIRE model as a 'major strength' (Reviewer 2) that 'for the first time, allows specific targeting of only fetal-derived macrophages.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'showed a reduction of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice' and acknowledges the 'robust methodology.' The specificity of the depletion to EMP-derived macrophages is accepted without critique.

result: Acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages using diphtheria toxin in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-DTR mice resulted in premature death within 24 hours and a systemic inflammatory response syndrome-like phenotype, demonstrating that acute depletion is not viable.
evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this finding is presented as justification for using the ΔFIRE model instead of DT-mediated depletion. Reviewers accept the ΔFIRE model without questioning why DT depletion was not used, implicitly supporting the rationale that acute DT depletion is problematic. No reviewer challenges these claims.

result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing revealed that two clusters of macrophages expressing homeostatic and antigen-presenting genes are specifically ablated in ΔFIRE mice, representing ~90% of YFP+ cells from the EMP lineage tracing model, while other macrophage clusters (Cx3cr1hi, Ccr2lowLy6clo, Ccr2hiLy6chi) and monocytes remain unaffected.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the authors 'characterized its macrophages populations via scRNAseq at baseline conditions' and acknowledges the 'robust methodology encompassing state of the art immunological methods.' Reviewer 2 states 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' implicitly accepting the scRNA-seq characterization of which populations are depleted.

result: Absence of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice is associated with changes in gene expression in non-macrophage immune cells (T-cells, B-cells, NK cells) and reduced overall phagocytic capacity.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk in response to injury,' directly supporting these claims about altered immune cell gene expression. No reviewer questions the phagocytosis score or changes in non-macrophage populations.

result: After I/R injury, cardiac function (LVEF and stroke volume) improved in control mice but remained unchanged or worsened in ΔFIRE mice from day 6 to day 30, indicating that absence of resident macrophages negatively influenced cardiac remodeling. However, infarct size (measured by PET viability defect and histological fibrosis) was not different between groups at 30 days.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'differential effects on echocardiographic function 6 and 30 days after I/R injury' and Reviewer 2 states 'the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' directly confirming both the functional impairment and the lack of difference in infarct size. All reviewers accept these findings without challenge.

result: After I/R injury, macrophages remain largely absent in the remote zone of ΔFIRE mice, but bone marrow-derived macrophages are recruited to the infarct area (representing ~75% of macrophages in the infarct zone, ~50% in border zone, and ~35% in remote zone at 30 days), with recruitment unaltered in ΔFIRE mice compared to controls.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'Via flow cytometry and histology the authors confirmed existing evidence of increased bone marrow-derived macrophage infiltration to the heart, specifically to the ischemic myocardium. Macrophage population in ΔFIRE mice after I/R injury were only changed in the remote zone.' This directly supports the spatial distribution and recruitment findings. No concerns are raised about the lineage tracing data showing BM-derived macrophage proportions.

result: Bulk RNA-sequencing of CD45.1+ (recruited) and CD45.2+ (resident) macrophages 2 days after I/R injury revealed profound transcriptional differences: resident macrophages upregulate homeostasis-related genes (Timd4, Lyve1, Cd163, Retnla) and development/homeostasis GO terms, while recruited macrophages upregulate inflammatory/host defense GO terms and processes related to innate and adaptive immunity.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'Further RNAseq data on resident or recruited macrophages showed transcriptional differences between both cell types in terms of homeostasis-related genes and inflammation.' This directly supports the bulk RNA-seq findings. Reviewer 2 states the findings are 'in line with the current idea in the field that macrophages of different origins have distinct functions in tissues,' affirming the biological interpretation.

result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing 2 days after I/R injury showed that homeostatic macrophages are reduced in ΔFIRE mice while Ccr2hiLy6chi inflammatory macrophages are unaltered. In ΔFIRE mice, anti-inflammatory genes (Chil3, Lcn2) are reduced and pro-apoptotic/inflammatory genes (Bcl2a1a, Bcl2a1d) are increased across immune cell clusters. Neutrophils show increased inflammasome activation, and ligand-receptor interactions from resident macrophage clusters to neutrophils/lymphocytes are markedly reduced, while BM-derived macrophage communication and transcriptional profiles remain unaltered.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states '2 days after I/R protocol ΔFIRE mice showed an enhanced pro inflammatory phenotype in the RNAseq data,' directly supporting the findings of altered inflammatory gene expression and neutrophil inflammasome activation. Reviewer 2 states 'the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk in response to injury,' confirming the ligand-receptor interaction findings. No concerns are raised about the scRNA-seq analysis after injury.

result: Pharmacological depletion of all macrophages (both resident and recruited) using CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 resulted in absence of cardiac macrophages within 7 days in healthy hearts and sustained depletion in all cardiac zones after I/R injury (without altering neutrophil recruitment). This was associated with increased infarct size, deteriorated cardiac function (reduced LVEF at both day 6 and day 30), demonstrating worse outcomes than ΔFIRE mice.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'Depleting all macrophage using a Csf1r inhibitor resulted in a reduced cardiac function and increased fibrosis,' directly supporting these findings. The comparison between ΔFIRE (resident only) and PLX5622 (resident + recruited) depletion is central to the manuscript's conclusions and is accepted by all reviewers without challenge.

result: By comparing ΔFIRE mice (resident macrophage depletion only) with PLX5622-treated mice (both resident and recruited macrophage depletion), the authors conclude that sole absence of resident macrophages has limited negative impact on cardiac remodeling, while absence of both populations results in significantly increased infarct size and deteriorated function. This demonstrates that recruited macrophages have a beneficial effect and determine infarct size, while resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses to improve cardiac remodeling.
evaluation: This is the central conclusion of the manuscript and is explicitly supported by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides important findings on the distinct functions exerted by resident and recruited macrophages during cardiac healing.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' and states the findings are 'in line with the current idea in the field that macrophages of different origins have distinct functions.' Reviewer 3 calls the work 'important for the field of cardiac injury.'
